881-practical-tips: Read the Admissions Policy, think about your motivations, and research law faculties so you can say why McGill. Don't restate your CV; be authentic and original without losing substance.

Write in whichever of English or French you express yourself best, or both; don't use it to prove bilingualism unless you're very comfortable. Check grammar and format, as you get only one submission. Indigenous applicants may add further documents.
881-format: 750 words at most, with the word count at the end. Put your name and McGill ID (from your acknowledgement) at the top right of each page. Re-applicants need a new statement; little change makes you unlikely to be competitive.
881-extenuating-circumstances: If a serious medical or personal difficulty affected your grades for a defined time, file this form. The Admissions Office weighs credibility and documents, dates, and which terms or courses were hit. It may then leave out affected results, at its sole discretion, and its decision is final.
881-format-2: Declare it in the application; a form then appears on your checklist. Attach at most two pages of supporting documents. One version only; later updates or mailed items aren't added.
881-cv: Cover academics, work, volunteering, activities, sports and interests, and languages. It helps show your strength, involvement, leadership and time management.
Give hours worked during your studies and time spent volunteering. Any work counts. Re-applicants must update it.
882-format: Any layout, two pages at most; nothing past that is read. An optional template is on the Admissions Guide's Supporting Documents page.
882-references: Exactly two, named in the first two Referee fields; each gets an email with instructions. You may substitute until the document deadline. Indigenous applicants should see their own page.

Students and recent students need professors or teachers who know their work; CEGEP and Quebec Baccalaureate applicants need two college professors. Otherwise use someone who supervises you and can judge reading, research and writing. Personal references don't help, and the office won't chase referees.
882-requirements: Forms must come from an institutional or corporate email, not Hotmail, Gmail, Yahoo, Sympatico or Videotron. Tell referees your category. You're responsible for timely receipt; check your Portal checklist rather than asking the office.
882-re-applicants: Since 2024–2025, name all referees in the Recommendations section, which sends the form. The same people may be used, but they must submit a new one.
882-law-school-admission-test-lsat: Optional, but any score counts. If you've taken it or will, report dates and your LSAT ID, even if you think it hurts you. Tell Admissions in writing about any later change. Files with pending results wait for review.
882-consequences-of-failure-to-disclose: Not disclosing the LSAT is material misrepresentation, which can cost you your offer or application at any time. Random checks run during admissions and systematic ones on those offered a place; offers have been revoked before.
Why not required: the test is only in English, which would disadvantage francophone applicants.

Should you take it: with about eight applicants per place, you should apply widely, and almost every law school outside Quebec requires it (except Ottawa's Civil Law and the French Common Law programs at Moncton and Ottawa). Consider it if your grades are below the admitted average GPA of 3.8 (about 85%).
McGill averages multiple sittings. Entering classes average 162: half between 160 and 164, a quarter between 150 and 160, a quarter above 164.
When: by November of the year before entry; results hold up your file. A January sitting risks no places being left. Your status stays "Items outstanding" until the score arrives.
883-processing-of-lsat-results: Results come straight from LSAC; reactivate your service if it expired. McGill doesn't run the test; register with LSAC. See the FAQ.
883-academic-regulations: This publication and Faculty Regulations govern Law students for 2026–2027, with any changes published before Fall registration. All may change at any time.
883-academic-standing: A credit system, detailed in the Registration Materials posted at mcgill.ca/law-studies/courses before Minerva opens in May. The Code of Student Conduct also applies.
883-academic-requirements: Finish within five years of first registering unless on approved leave (Reg. 5) or part-time (Reg. 53). You can't also be in a Bar training program (Reg. 4). Full-time means 12+ credits a term, except a final term needing fewer (Reg. 3). No credit for courses counted toward another degree (Reg. 10).
Expect two hours of study per lecture hour, plus essays, seminars and Legal Methodology. No other studies during the session without the Dean's approval.

Evaluation is anonymous (Regs. 19, 22). Write in English or French; exam questions follow the course language but may include either (Reg. 20). If you don't pass a session you must withdraw, but may apply for readmission (Regs. 49, 50).
883-admission-to-the-legal-profession: The Career Development Office tracks Bar rules for common jurisdictions, but meeting them, including pre-law education, is your job.
884-admission-to-the-legal-profession-ca: See each regulator's site. The National Committee on Accreditation, at flsc.ca, handles moves between provincial bars; Comités des équivalences handle transfers to Quebec.
884-admission-to-the-legal-profession-th: The J.D. is approved in some jurisdictions (such as NY and MA), so graduates proceed like US students, with a Foreign Legal Education Evaluation for New York. Some states also need particular pre-law study, so check early; the CDO has information.
884-overview-of-undergraduate-degrees-of: One integrated program gives both the B.C.L. and the J.D. You may add a minor, major or honours, do a joint degree in Management or Social Work, go on exchange, earn non-course or outside credits, or take internships.
884-mcgill-b-c-l-j-d-program: First-year transsystemic teaching covers both traditions in one course, building analysis and openness. 105 credits, usually in 3.5–4 years, or 3 with summer courses and heavier loads.
You can't combine it with another university program, go part-time to pursue other studies, or take leave for a graduate program.
884-m-b-a-law-program: With Desautels. Apply separately to Law and to the M.B.A.; see mcgill.ca/law-studies/bcljd-studies/joint-MBA.
884-m-s-w-law-program: With the School of Social Work. Apply separately to each; see mcgill.ca/law-studies/bcljd-studies/joint-MSW.
884-exchange-and-study-abroad-options-fo: About 25% of undergraduates go abroad. McGill students: see the Student Affairs Office. Students from elsewhere: see Incoming Exchange and Visiting Students. General information is on p. 1286.
Credited summer Human Rights Internships run through the Centre for Human Rights and Legal Pluralism; see mcgill.ca/humanrights/clinical/internships and mcgill.ca/cdo.
885-student-activities-and-services: Many activities and clubs, mostly under the Law Students Association: lsa-aed.ca.
885-clinical-legal-education-at-mcgill-l: Up to 15 non-course credits for practical learning: human rights internships, court clerkships, mooting, the Legal Clinic Course, law journals, and work as a Legal Methodology Tutorial Leader or Group Assistant.
885-student-affairs-office: New Chancellor Day Hall, Room 433: the Associate Dean (Academic), Assistant Dean (Students), Student Affairs Officer, two Student Advisors and coordinators, helping at every stage.
885-student-advising-and-support: Help with stress, productivity, sleep, money or personal problems; drop by or email sao.law@mcgill.ca, and point classmates who struggle here too. Also advice on registration, planning, part-time status, leave, exams, majors, honours, minors, exchanges and summer courses.
885-academic-accommodations: Options include extensions, deferrals, attendance waivers, leave and part-time study. Ask the Student Affairs Office, not your instructors, and bring documents. Student Accessibility and Achievement helps with disabilities and health conditions, temporary or lasting; book through ClockWork.
885-scholarships-and-financial-support: The Faculty's awards recognize academics and activities. The Scholarships and Student Aid Office offers aid to full-time degree students: counsellors assess need and guide you to grants, loans, government aid and campus jobs.
885-student-wellness: Workshops in the Academic Success Series, wellness events, and a site on health, money, volunteering, dependents and mentorship. Local Wellness Advisors offer programming, single one-on-one sessions and training for student groups.
886-law-students-association-association: Founded March 12, 1912 and incorporated May 4, 1992, now about 600 members, up from 30. The official Law student body, representing you in the Faculty and beyond and running services and events. Nine elected executives; office in the basement of Old Chancellor Day Hall.
886-legal-information-clinic-at-mcgill: Free, bilingual, student-run legal information, referrals and document certification for McGill and Montreal, with a focus on marginalized groups. Law students past first year can volunteer. SSMU Building, Room 107, 3480 McTavish St.; 514-398-6792; licm.ca.
886-contours: A student magazine since 2012 on women and law, in writing and art. Published yearly in English and French.
886-graduate-law-student-association: Five executives represent all graduate Law students and postdocs at the Faculty and PGSS, sitting on committees and running social and academic events.
886-innocence-mcgill: Since 2005, a student-run clinic with a supervising lawyer and Faculty Advisor, investigating wrongful conviction claims for serious crimes in Quebec.
886-l-e-x-program: Formerly High School Outreach. Law students and Montreal-area teens learn from each other, responding to dropout rates and the under-representation of underprivileged, immigrant and minority youth.
886-mcgill-journal-of-law-and-health: A peer-reviewed, bilingual, student-run journal since 2007 on health law and policy, from medical technology to ethics.
887-mcgill-journal-of-sustainable-develo: Formerly the International Journal of Sustainable Development Law and Policy. Student-run and peer-reviewed since 2004, connecting law, development, environment, economics and society.
887-mcgill-law-journal: Student-founded in 1952: critical analysis of public, private and international law, in common and civil law, for professors, lawyers and students.
887-mcgill-journal-of-dispute-resolution: Peer-reviewed since 2014, on domestic and international alternative dispute resolution.
887-pro-bono-students-canada: Founded at Toronto in 1996, now at all 22 Canadian law schools: 1,600 volunteers give about 140,000 free hours to over 400 groups, courts and tribunals yearly. The McGill chapter started in 2000, and in 2012–2013 had 91 volunteers with 32 Montreal organizations.
887-quid-novi: The Faculty's weekly paper, funded by the LSA, with news, satire, poetry and commentary.
887-skit-nite: A yearly student comedy and music show, raising money for Montreal charities.
887-scholarships-prizes-and-student-aid-: The Undergraduate Scholarships and Awards Calendar lists all SSAO aid. Links cover entrance and in-course awards, Law's discretionary prizes, bursaries and loans, and Work Study.
887-career-development-office: Career counselling, led by a lawyer alumnus with a career advisor and Associate: summer jobs, articling and post-graduation options. Employers can post free on myFuture and join on-campus interviews and events.
888-career-days-for-law-students: Six a year: career paths, public interest (November, with panels), Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto and US employers.
888-on-campus-recruitment-for-the-facult: On-campus interviews: US (August), Vancouver and Calgary (September), Toronto (October), Ottawa (January), with processes for other cities. Montreal's Course aux stages happens at firms' offices, with step-by-step CDO help.
888-resource-centre-of-the-faculty-of-la: Publications on job searches, diversity and employers, a website, and the myFuture job tool.
888-faculty-of-law-training-programs-and: Seminars, one-on-one counselling, newsletters for each recruitment process, mock interviews, guides, and panels and networking with alumni.
888-program-requirements: After four terms with a GPA of 3.0. Add 15 Honours Thesis credits to the 105; the distinction depends on an approved thesis.
889-any-year: One 1-credit course, any year after first.
890-elective-courses-46-credits: Faculty courses or approved equivalents, to reach 120 credits.
890-minimum-writing-requirement: One research paper, solo, through a course essay worth 75%+ of the grade, a supervised for-credit term essay, or an equivalent piece accepted by the McGill Law Journal with its Adviser's approval.
890-program-requirements: Qualifies you for Bar programs in all Canadian provinces. Both degrees are granted together at 105 credits. See mcgill.ca/law-studies for updates.
891-program-requirements: Any Law student may add an Arts minor concentration, Science minor, or Desautels minor for non-Management students. See those faculties for requirements.
892-b-c-l-and-j-d-with-minor: 18 credits beyond the 105. For a 24-credit Science minor, 6 credits count toward Law as non-Law credits.
893-program-description: With Desautels: legal and administrative sides of business, leading to the M.B.A., B.C.L. and J.D., for private, public and government careers. 39 credits of M.B.A. and 93 of B.C.L./J.D., 132 in all.
893-elective-courses-15-credits: 600-level Faculty courses, approved by an adviser. Attend M.B.A. Base Camp (Accounting and Business Math) before starting.
895-elective-courses-34-credits: Faculty courses or approved equivalents, to reach the 93 credits.
895-program-description: With the School of Social Work: 45 credits of M.S.W. and 87 of B.C.L./J.D., 132 in all.
895-complementary-courses-social-work-15: 500- or 600-level SWRK. Up to 6 graduate credits outside the School with the Academic Adviser's approval.
896-elective-courses-28-credits: Faculty courses or approved equivalents, to reach 132 credits.
897-program-description: Open to all Law students: interdisciplinary law and non-law courses, an internship and an essay. 36 credits: 18 fit within the 105 and 18 are added, for 123 in all.
897-essay-course: On the major's topic, in the fourth year, with a topic approved by the Associate Dean (Academic).
898-non-law-courses: 6–12 credits. Taking 6 lets you count 6 more toward the law degrees; taking 9 lets you count 3; taking 12 allows none. Others with the Program Adviser's approval.
898-essay-course-3-credits: On the major's topic, in the fourth year, with a topic approved by the Associate Dean (Academic).
899-non-law-courses: 6–12 credits. Taking 6 lets you count 6 more toward the law degrees; taking 9 lets you count 3; taking 12 allows none. Others with the Program Adviser's approval.
900-undergraduate-selection-of-course-co: Unofficial groupings of regular courses to help you pick electives; not a Faculty policy. Some courses appear in several, so read the course descriptions.
900-basic-private-law: LAWG 100D1/D2 Contractual Obligations; LAWG 101D1/D2 Extra-Contractual Obligations/Torts.
900-advanced-private-law: Civil law: PROC 200, LAWG 506, BUS2 561, PRV2 270, PROC 549.
Common law: PRV3 200, PRV5 582, PRV4 549, PRV4 451, PRV3 534, PRV4 500.
Transsystemic: BUS2 365, LAWG 200, PRV5 483, LAWG 504, LEEL 570, LAWG 415, LAWG 273, LAWG 300, CMPL 522, LAWG 316, LAWG 220D1/D2, LAWG 400.
